opening.spoken: This record covers the claimed solution of Erdős problem #593: what has been claimed, what it rests on, and what would have to be checked by whom.

short_version.spoken: Erdős asked which finite 3-uniform hypergraphs must appear in every 3-uniform hypergraph of uncountable chromatic number, a five-hundred-dollar problem. In June and July 2026 two claimants, Eric Li and Samuil Petkov, each working with an AI system, listed proofs reaching the same characterisation, each with a Lean development. Two claims that agree is more than one, and still nobody independent has reported building either development or reading either argument. Everything here is open.

what_happened.spoken: The claim was pinned from the public record: the problem page, the proof-claims thread, and every artifact the claimants made public, by commit or hash. Nothing was run. A reading guide now lays the third-party formal statement and both claimants' main theorems beside the problem as posed, definition by definition, so the human read of what the statements say takes under an hour.

do_not_rely_on.spoken: the claimed solution as settled; nothing in it has standing yet

certainty_statement.spoken: Nothing is certified or accepted. Every item is open.

cycles.spoken: Eric Li posted a paper on arXiv claiming to resolve problems 593 and 1177; the Erdős-problems AI wiki listed it as a candidate full solution, marked unverified. Samuil Petkov listed a proof claim reaching the same characterisation, stating it had been checked by AI models and not by an expert. Eric Li listed his proof claim on the problem page. Eric Li's Lean repository reached its current commit. Samuil Petkov's repository reached its current commit, with a Lean formalisation under a formalization folder. The problem page lists two proof claims, neither marked accepted by the site. A third-party formalisation of the problem statement exists.

predictions: P1: no claimant states or imports the formal-conjectures theorem; no pair of statements is textually identical

P2: the two claimants' statements are equivalent in content (same 'appears', same threshold, same answer as an iff, both via deletion of isolated vertices), and each fills the formal-conjectures blank

P3: at least three conventions need a sentence (host universe, Petkov's edge-index type, Fin n labelling); none changes the meaning; the sharpest human point is whether the answer is a characterisation in Erdős's sense
P4: no meaning-changing discrepancy is seen

numbers.pairwise_reading: Li vs Petkov equivalent; each claimant vs formal-conjectures: same left-hand side, fills its blank answer; no pair identical

misses: P3 named the right conventions but the sharpest human point turned out to be the non-induced reading of 'appear in' (checklist A1) as much as the form of the characterisation (A3).
Not foreseen: the record's own claim file was wrong that Petkov has no lakefile (it is under formalization/), and gap EG4's word 'independently' overstates what Petkov's README claims (D11, D12).

cycles.spoken: Nervous Machine wrote the reading guide for the two questions on this record that a machine cannot settle: whether the formal statements of problem 593 say what Erdős asked, and whether the two claimants' Lean theorems say the same thing. The guide quotes the problem page, the third-party formal statement and both claimants' main theorems word for word, traces every symbol to its definition in the claimants' files and in Mathlib with file and line, and lays the three side by side. In the agent's reading the two claimants state the same theorem in different encodings, and each fills the blank that the third-party statement leaves for the answer. Thirteen differences are written down; none changes the meaning. The one interpretive choice all three share is that "appear in" means a copy that need not be induced. Nothing was built or run, the Lean examples are written but not yet checked, and the readings are the system's, not a mathematician's, so nothing changed standing. A combinatorialist can now sign or refuse four lines in under an hour.

background.spoken: A 3-uniform hypergraph has chromatic number greater than aleph-null if its vertices cannot be coloured with countably many colours without a monochromatic edge. Which finite 3-uniform hypergraphs appear inside every such hypergraph? For ordinary graphs Erdős considered the question solved: uncountably chromatic graphs contain every finite bipartite graph but need not contain any fixed odd cycle.

background.spoken: The claim characterises the obligatory finite triple systems: after deleting isolated vertices, exactly the linear systems in which every hyperedge-node meets a bridge in the Levi graph and every Berge cycle has even length. The author states that the argument was checked by AI models several times and not by an expert, and that a formalisation was under way at submission; the repository now holds a Lean formalisation.

provenance.source: public record to 2026-11-14: the problem page, its proof-claims thread and the claimants' public artifacts, pinned in claim.yaml

background.spoken: The claim resolves problems 593 and 1177 together. The obligatory finite triple systems are exactly the class generated from private-vertex expansions of finite bipartite graphs by finite disjoint unions and one-point amalgamations, equivalently the linear systems with a bridge at every hyperedge-node of the Levi graph and only even Berge cycles. The proof uses an exact bridge-trace theorem for one-apex sequence lifts, and also constructs, for every uncountable cardinal, a linear triple system of exactly that chromatic number. The author states the paper was public on arXiv on June 23, 2026, before any other proof of 593 or 1177, and welcomes others to join the formalisation.
